html:
Travel nursing sounds exciting until the housing question comes up. Where do you sleep for the next 13 weeks. Who covers that cost.

This is the question that trips up most new travel nurses. You get a job offer. The pay rate looks great. Then housing enters the conversation and things get confusing fast.

This guide breaks down exactly who pays for housing, how the models work, and what to watch for before you sign anything.

What Travel Nurse Housing Actually Means

Travel nurse housing refers to your living arrangement during a temporary assignment. Contracts typically run 8 to 13 weeks. Some stretch to six months.

You’re not relocating permanently. You’re working somewhere temporarily, then moving to the next assignment or heading home.

This creates a housing problem regular employment doesn’t have. A permanent nurse signs a year-long lease near their hospital. A travel nurse can’t do that. Three months isn’t enough time to justify a full lease in most cases.

Agencies solved this problem by building housing support directly into their contracts. That support comes in different forms. Understanding which form you’re getting changes your entire financial picture.

Housing isn’t a small line item either. In major Canadian cities, a furnished short-term rental can cost more per month than a mortgage payment. If your contract doesn’t account for that properly, your take-home pay shrinks fast.

This is why every travel nurse needs to understand the payment model before accepting an assignment. Not after. Before.

The Three Common Payment Models

Most Canadian staffing agencies use one of three approaches to housing. Some mix elements of all three depending on the assignment.

Agency-Provided Housing

In this model, the agency books and pays for your housing directly. You don’t handle the lease. You don’t hunt for apartments. You don’t pay a deposit.

The agency typically partners with corporate housing providers or extended-stay properties. These units come furnished. Kitchen included. Utilities usually included. Sometimes even parking included.

You receive a housing package as part of your offer. Your job is to show up and unpack.

This model suits nurses who are new to travel work. It removes the guesswork. It also removes a lot of the stress that comes with finding short-term housing in an unfamiliar city.

There are tradeoffs. You don’t get to choose your building or neighborhood. You share the space if the agency assigns roommates to cut costs. Some contracts allow you to decline agency housing and take a stipend instead, but not all.

Agency-provided housing also means less flexibility. If you want to bring a pet, or you need a specific layout, you may not get it. The agency picks based on availability and cost, not your preferences.

Still, this option removes financial risk. You know the cost is covered. You’re not fronting money and hoping for reimbursement later.

Housing Stipends

This is the most common model for experienced travel nurses. Instead of the agency booking your housing, they give you a stipend.

A stipend is a set amount of money added to your pay package. It’s meant to cover housing costs. In Canada, this stipend is often structured to be tax-free under certain conditions, provided you maintain a permanent tax home elsewhere and meet CRA requirements for temporary work assignments.

You find your own housing. You sign your own short-term lease or book your own furnished rental. You keep whatever money is left over after covering your costs.

This is where travel nurses can actually increase their take-home income. If your stipend is $2,200 a month and you find a place for $1,600, that extra $600 is yours.

The flip side is real too. If you can’t find affordable housing and rent runs higher than your stipend, you absorb the difference. This happens often in cities like Toronto, Vancouver, and Calgary, where short-term rental prices spike during peak seasons.

Stipend amounts vary based on location. Agencies typically calculate a fair market rate for furnished short-term housing in that specific city. A stipend for a placement in a small Ontario town looks very different from one in downtown Vancouver.

Ask your recruiter how the stipend was calculated. A transparent agency will explain their methodology. A vague answer is worth questioning.

Self-Booked Housing with Reimbursement

In this third model, you book and pay for housing yourself first. The agency reimburses you afterward, usually against receipts and a housing budget cap.

This gives you maximum control. You choose the location. You choose the building. You choose your roommates, if any.

It also means more work on your end. You need to research housing options before your contract even starts. You need to submit receipts. You need to track spending carefully so you don’t exceed your reimbursement cap.

Cash flow becomes a real consideration here. You’re often paying rent upfront and waiting for reimbursement on your next pay cycle. If you don’t have savings to cover that gap, this model creates financial strain.

Some nurses prefer this model anyway. It offers the most flexibility. You can negotiate a better rate than the agency might get through their corporate housing partners. You can also choose a location closer to the facility, cutting your commute significantly.

Read your reimbursement terms carefully. Know your cap. Know your deadline for submitting receipts. Missing a deadline can mean losing reimbursement entirely.

A Quick Side-by-Side Example

Picture three nurses accepting similar 13-week contracts in the same city.

Nurse A takes agency-provided housing. She pays nothing directly. Her paycheck reflects her hourly wage only. Housing risk sits entirely with the agency.

Nurse B takes a stipend of $2,400 a month. She finds a rental for $1,900. She pockets the $500 difference every month, adding roughly $1,500 to her total earnings across the contract.

Nurse C books her own housing at $2,600 a month and gets reimbursed against a $2,300 cap. She covers the $300 gap herself, reducing her effective take-home pay.

Same contract length. Same city. Three very different financial outcomes, based entirely on the housing model and how well each nurse managed it.

This example shows why housing terms deserve as much attention as your hourly rate. The model you choose can shift your real earnings by thousands of dollars over a single assignment.

How Staffing Agencies Handle Housing Costs

Housing never appears out of nowhere in your contract. Agencies build it into your total compensation package from the start.

When an agency posts a job, they calculate a full package. This includes your hourly rate, any overtime provisions, travel reimbursement, and housing support. All of it gets bundled into what recruiters call your “total package value.”

This matters because two contracts with different hourly rates can actually offer the same total value once housing is factored in. A lower hourly rate with generous housing support might beat a higher hourly rate with a thin stipend.

Some agencies work with dedicated housing coordinators. These coordinators handle logistics for agency-provided housing, negotiate rates with corporate housing providers, and troubleshoot issues like maintenance requests or lease extensions.

Other agencies keep things simpler. They calculate a stipend based on GSA-style rate tables or local market averages, then leave the rest to you.

Ask your recruiter directly which approach their agency uses. Get the answer in writing, ideally in your contract, not just in a verbal conversation.

A red flag worth watching for is any agency that’s vague about how housing is calculated. If they can’t explain their numbers clearly, that’s a sign to ask more questions before signing.

Larger agencies often maintain standing relationships with corporate housing companies in major Canadian cities. These relationships let them lock in better rates than an individual nurse could find on their own. Smaller or newer agencies may not have these partnerships yet, which sometimes means thinner stipends or less reliable housing options.

It’s worth asking how long an agency has operated in your target city. An agency with years of experience placing nurses in Toronto likely has stronger housing infrastructure than one just entering that market.

Some agencies also offer a hybrid approach. They provide a base housing option through a corporate partner, but let you opt out for a cash stipend instead if you’d rather manage your own arrangement. This flexibility benefits nurses who want the security of a backup option while still controlling their own housing choice.

How Provinces and Health Authorities Factor In

Housing support isn’t uniform across Canada. It shifts depending on the province, the health authority, and even the specific facility you’re assigned to.

Public health authorities in provinces like Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta often negotiate staffing contracts separately from private facilities. These contracts sometimes include housing provisions baked directly into the agreement between the health authority and the staffing agency.

Rural and remote placements tend to come with stronger housing perks. Northern Ontario, rural Saskatchewan, and remote parts of British Columbia all struggle to recruit permanent staff. Health authorities in these regions often sweeten travel nurse contracts to compensate.

This happens for a simple reason. Rural facilities can’t compete with city hospitals on lifestyle or amenities. Better housing support, sometimes fully covered, becomes the incentive that gets nurses to take the assignment.

Urban placements work differently. Cities like Toronto and Vancouver have no shortage of applicants for most positions, so housing incentives tend to be smaller relative to the cost of living in those markets. This creates a strange imbalance where your stipend might feel generous in a rural town but tight in a major city.

Provincial healthcare funding models also play a role. Provinces with centralized health authorities, like Alberta Health Services, negotiate staffing contracts differently than provinces with more fragmented regional health boards. This affects how consistently housing terms are applied across facilities within the same province.

Always ask which health authority or facility you’re being placed with. Then ask if housing terms are standard across that authority or negotiated per assignment. The answer changes what you should expect.

A Province-by-Province Snapshot

Ontario. Housing costs vary wildly across this province. Toronto and the Greater Toronto Area push stipends higher due to expensive short-term rentals. Northern Ontario facilities, including Sudbury and Thunder Bay, often offer stronger incentives to attract staff.

British Columbia. Vancouver and Victoria carry some of the highest housing costs in the country. Agencies working in these markets typically build larger stipends into their offers. Interior and northern BC placements often come with more generous support due to staffing shortages.

Alberta. Alberta Health Services runs a more centralized system than many provinces. This can mean more consistent housing terms across facilities within the same health zone. Rural Alberta placements still tend to offer stronger perks than Calgary or Edmonton.

Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Housing costs run lower here compared to coastal provinces. Stipends reflect that lower cost of living. Rural placements in both provinces often include added housing incentives to offset isolation.

Atlantic Canada. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador all face significant nursing shortages, particularly outside major cities. Housing incentives in these provinces have grown in recent years as health authorities compete harder for travel nurses.

Quebec. Language requirements add a layer of complexity here. Housing terms still follow similar patterns to the rest of the country. Montreal carries higher costs. Remote regions of the province often offer stronger support.

This snapshot changes over time as staffing shortages shift. Always confirm current terms directly with your recruiter rather than relying on general trends.

What Affects Your Housing Budget

Several factors shape how much you’ll actually spend on housing during an assignment, regardless of which payment model your agency uses.

Location

This is the single biggest factor. Housing in downtown Toronto costs significantly more than housing in a small town in Manitoba.

Furnished short-term rentals in major cities often run $2,500 to $4,000 a month. The same style of rental in a smaller city or town might run $1,200 to $1,800.

Your stipend should reflect this difference. If it doesn’t, question the number before accepting the contract.

Assignment Length

Shorter contracts often come with higher weekly housing costs. Landlords and corporate housing providers charge premium rates for stays under three months.

A six-month assignment might unlock better housing rates than an eight-week assignment in the same city. This is worth factoring into your decision if you have flexibility on contract length.

Season and Demand

Housing prices shift with seasonal demand, especially in cities that attract tourism or seasonal workers. Summer months in cities like Vancouver or Halifax often mean higher short-term rental prices.

If your assignment falls during a high-demand season, your stipend might not stretch as far as it would during a quieter month.

Contract Terms

Every agency structures housing differently, and every contract spells out different specifics. Some cap reimbursement amounts. Some include utilities in agency-provided housing. Others don’t.

Read every clause related to housing before signing. Don’t assume standard terms apply across agencies. They don’t.

How to Estimate a Fair Housing Stipend Yourself

You don’t need to take an agency’s stipend number at face value. A little research lets you check it against real market rates.

Start by searching furnished short-term rental listings in your assignment city. Sites that list corporate housing and extended-stay units give a realistic monthly range for your specific location.

Compare that range against the stipend you’ve been offered. If the stipend sits well below typical furnished rental costs, you’ll likely need to cover a gap out of pocket.

Factor in the length of your assignment too. Very short contracts, under eight weeks, often carry higher weekly housing rates because landlords price in the inconvenience of a short-term tenant.

Check for seasonal price spikes as well. A summer assignment in a tourist-heavy city can mean higher rental costs than the same assignment during a quieter month.

Once you have a realistic number, bring it back to your recruiter. Ask directly if the stipend can be adjusted based on your research. Agencies sometimes have more flexibility than their initial offer suggests, especially for hard-to-fill positions.

This small amount of homework puts you in a stronger negotiating position. It also protects you from accepting a contract that looks good on paper but leaves you short once real housing costs are factored in.

Tax Implications of Housing Stipends in Canada

Housing stipends can be tax-free under Canadian tax law, but only under specific conditions set by the Canada Revenue Agency.

To qualify, you generally need to maintain a permanent tax home separate from your assignment location. This usually means keeping a primary residence you return to between contracts and continuing to pay expenses there.

You also need to be working away from that tax home temporarily, not permanently relocating. If the CRA considers your assignment location your new permanent tax home, your stipend could become taxable income.

This is a nuanced area of tax law, and rules can vary based on your specific situation. Speaking with an accountant familiar with travel nurse contracts is worth the cost. A wrong assumption here can mean an unexpected tax bill at year end.

Keep documentation throughout your assignments. Save your lease agreements. Save records showing you maintained your permanent residence. This paperwork protects you if the CRA ever questions your tax filing.

Agencies aren’t tax advisors, and their explanations of stipend taxation shouldn’t replace professional advice. Treat their guidance as a starting point, not a final answer.

Documentation to Keep Throughout Your Assignment

Good record-keeping protects you financially and legally during every assignment. Build this habit from your very first contract.

Keep a copy of every signed lease or rental agreement. This proves your housing costs if a dispute comes up with your agency.

Save every receipt tied to reimbursable housing expenses. Photograph them immediately in case a paper copy gets lost or fades.

Track your permanent residence expenses separately. This includes mortgage or rent payments, utility bills, and any other proof you maintain a home base outside your assignment location.

Keep copies of every contract and any written correspondence about housing terms. Email confirmations count. Screenshots of text messages from your recruiter count too, especially if verbal promises differ from what’s in your formal contract.

Store all of this digitally, ideally in a dedicated folder you back up regularly. Travel nurses move often, and physical paperwork gets lost easily between assignments.

This documentation matters most in two scenarios. The first is a tax audit, where the CRA may ask for proof you maintained a permanent tax home. The second is a contract dispute, where written proof of agreed terms protects you if an agency tries to change conditions after the fact.

Common Housing Mistakes New Travel Nurses Make

New travel nurses often make the same handful of mistakes when it comes to housing. Avoiding these early saves money and stress later.

Not comparing total package value. Focusing only on hourly rate while ignoring housing terms leads to accepting a worse overall deal. Always calculate the full package before comparing offers.

Assuming stipends are guaranteed income. A stipend covers housing costs. Spending it as if it’s pure bonus income, without securing housing first, creates a cash crunch fast.

Skipping the fine print on reimbursement caps. Self-booked housing arrangements often come with strict caps and documentation deadlines. Missing these details means losing money you expected to get back.

Not asking about roommate policies. Agency-provided housing sometimes includes shared units to cut costs. Nurses who assume private housing get an unwelcome surprise on arrival.

Ignoring lease flexibility for extensions. Assignments get extended often. Nurses who book rigid short-term leases without extension options sometimes scramble to find new housing mid-contract.

Forgetting to ask about utilities. Some housing packages include utilities. Others don’t. This gap can add hundreds of dollars a month to your actual cost of living.

Booking housing too far from the facility. A cheaper rental across town sounds appealing until commute times and parking costs eat into the savings. Factor in transportation costs when comparing housing options, not just the rent itself.

Not confirming internet and cell coverage. Rural placements sometimes come with limited connectivity. Nurses who rely on video calls with family or streaming for downtime should confirm this before committing to a specific rental.

Tips for Nurses Negotiating Housing Terms

Before accepting any contract, ask your recruiter these questions directly.

Does the stipend cover utilities. Is furniture included in agency-provided housing. What happens to housing arrangements if the assignment gets extended. What happens if the assignment ends early. Is there a reimbursement cap, and what’s the deadline for submitting receipts. Are roommates part of the agency housing arrangement. How was the stipend amount calculated for this specific location.

Get every answer in writing. Verbal promises from a recruiter don’t hold up if a dispute comes up later.

Compare offers from more than one agency whenever possible. Housing terms vary more than most new travel nurses expect, even for similar assignments in the same city.

Watch for vague language in your contract. Phrases like “housing assistance provided” without specific dollar amounts or terms should raise questions. Ask for clarity before signing.

Talk to other travel nurses who’ve worked with the same agency. Online forums and Facebook groups for Canadian travel nurses are full of firsthand accounts of how specific agencies handle housing in practice.

Finally, don’t be afraid to negotiate. Housing terms aren’t always fixed. If you have leverage, whether that’s a hard-to-fill specialty or a rural placement agencies struggle to staff, use it to negotiate better housing terms.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does every travel nurse agency in Canada offer housing stipends. No. Some agencies only offer agency-provided housing. Others only offer stipends. Ask directly before assuming.

Can I negotiate a higher housing stipend. Sometimes. This depends on the agency, the location, and how in-demand your specialty is. It never hurts to ask.

What happens if I can’t find housing within my stipend amount. You absorb the difference in most stipend models. This is why researching housing costs before accepting a contract matters so much.

Are housing stipends always tax-free. Not automatically. Specific CRA conditions apply. Speak with an accountant to confirm your situation qualifies.

Do rural placements always offer better housing support. Often, but not always. It depends on the health authority and how difficult that specific location is to staff.

What’s the difference between a stipend and a per diem. A stipend usually refers to a fixed monthly housing allowance. A per diem often covers daily living expenses like meals, separate from housing. Some contracts combine both terms loosely, so always ask your recruiter to define each one clearly.

Can I bring my family on a travel nursing assignment. Yes, though this affects your housing needs significantly. A stipend calculated for a single nurse won’t stretch as far for a family unit. Discuss your situation with your recruiter before accepting an offer.

What happens to my housing if my contract gets cancelled early. This depends entirely on your contract terms. Some agencies cover early termination costs for agency-provided housing. Others leave you responsible for breaking a lease. Ask this question before signing, not after a cancellation happens.

Should I choose agency-provided housing or a stipend as a first-time travel nurse. Agency-provided housing removes a lot of stress for first-time travelers. Once you’re comfortable navigating short-term rentals, a stipend often becomes more financially rewarding.

Do housing terms differ between agency staff and unionized permanent staff at the same facility. Yes, often significantly. Permanent unionized staff negotiate housing and relocation terms through collective agreements. Travel nurses negotiate housing terms directly with their staffing agency, which follows a completely separate process.

A Pre-Contract Housing Checklist

Before signing your next contract, run through this list.

Confirm which payment model applies to your assignment. Get the stipend amount or reimbursement cap in writing. Ask whether utilities and furniture are included. Ask about roommate policies for agency-provided housing. Confirm what happens if your contract extends or ends early. Research actual short-term rental costs in your assignment city. Speak with an accountant about your specific tax situation. Save all documentation related to your housing arrangement.

Running through this checklist takes fifteen minutes. Skipping it can cost you hundreds of dollars a month.

Why This Question Matters More Than It Seems

Housing feels like a secondary detail when you’re excited about a new assignment. It isn’t.

A strong hourly rate paired with weak housing terms can leave you worse off than a modest rate with solid housing support. The full package always tells the real story.

Nurses who treat housing terms as seriously as pay rate tend to have smoother assignments. Fewer surprises. Fewer disputes. More predictable take-home pay from contract to contract.

Make this part of your standard process every time you evaluate a new offer. It takes a little extra time upfront. It saves real money and real stress down the line.

Final Thoughts

Housing shouldn’t be a surprise halfway through your assignment. Know your payment model before you sign anything.

Ask direct questions early. Get every answer in writing. Compare full package value, not just hourly rate.

The nurses who navigate travel assignments successfully aren’t the ones who got lucky. They’re the ones who asked the right questions upfront.
